w: What's tested Sexual differentiation: why the female tract is the default pathway, and what happens to the Müllerian and Wolffian ducts The ovary's zones, and how the follicle and its oocyte develop, from primordial follicle to corpus luteum Steroid production in the follicle (two cells, two gonadotropins: he called it a very important slide), the three estrogens, and what estradiol and progesterone do The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis: GnRH, FSH, LH, inhibin, KNDy neurons, and the switch from negative to positive feedback The menstrual cycle: follicular phase, the LH surge and ovulation, luteal phase and menses, with the matching changes in the uterus and cervix (comparing the follicular and luteal phases is "high yield for exam") Menopause, and the reproductive disorders on the last slide 1 Exam 2 in-class review (11/11): progesterone rules the luteal phase, FSH raises aromatase, high estradiol sets off the LH surge; and their twins Exam 2 review · 6 questions in the bank Know this LH turns up cholesterol desmolase (P450scc), the rate-limiting step, cholesterol to pregnenolone, in the theca cells; FSH turns up aromatase, testosterone to 17-beta estradiol, in the granulosa cells. Aromatase is in males too, but far more active in females. Estrogen can give both. At ordinary levels it suppresses GnRH, LH and FSH. But as follicles grow and estradiol keeps rising, it progressively sensitizes the pituitary to GnRH, so that just before ovulation GnRH sets off a burst of LH. That amplification of the pituitary's response is positive feedback. Theca cells respond to LH. LH increases the activity of cholesterol desmolase, also called P450scc or the side-chain cleavage enzyme, which turns cholesterol into pregnenolone. It is the rate-limiting step of estrogen synthesis, and the theca cells make testosterone, the precursor of estrogen (and some progesterone along the way). Theca cells have no aromatase, so their testosterone moves over to the granulosa cells. In class he added that the endometrial vasculature thickens and glycogen vacuoles form, so an embryo that implants has blood supply and an energy store, and that the thick mucus suits implantation rather than sperm. One more sign: progesterone acts on the hypothalamus to raise body temperature, so a slight rise in temperature, a "slight fever," is a feature of the luteal phase. 3 Two cells, two gonadotropins: FSH, granulosa, aromatase, estradiol; LH, theca, cholesterol desmolase (P450scc, the rate-limiting step), testosterone; theca like Leydig, granulosa like Sertoli Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this FSH binds the granulosa cells (they carry the FSH receptors) and turns up aromatase, so testosterone becomes 17-beta estradiol. LH binds the theca cells, which make some progesterone and a lot of testosterone and have no aromatase; that testosterone moves to the granulosa cells. Theca is like Leydig, granulosa like Sertoli. The cells of the male lecture map straight on: theca cells are like Leydig cells (LH, testosterone), and granulosa cells are like Sertoli cells (FSH, aromatase). Each half depends on the other. Block LH and the theca cells stop supplying testosterone, so aromatase has nothing to convert. Block FSH and testosterone is still made, but it is not turned into estradiol. Ovulation follows a burst of estradiol. The loop is the same as in the follicular phase, GnRH to FSH and LH to estradiol, until plasma estradiol reaches a critical level, greater than 200 picograms per milliliter. That prompts the positive feedback mechanism, which sets off the surge of LH, and the surge causes ovulation. FSH rises along with it, but far less. In class he asked why, and answered it: as the follicle develops, inhibin rises, and inhibin "is going to preferentially inhibit FSH," feeding back on the anterior pituitary, "so that's why we don't call it an LH-FSH surge, we call it an LH surge." That agrees with Dr. Herr's cycle graph in L14, where FSH makes a small peak beside the LH surge, and with the slide's "FSH is suppressed by production of inhibin." 5 Ovulation: LH receptors on the preovulatory follicle, collagenase and prostaglandins, OMI falls and meiosis I resumes, 14 days before menses Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this The surge acts on that follicle three ways: proteases such as collagenase weaken its wall, prostaglandins raise its blood flow, and oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI) falls, so meiosis I resumes and is finished by ovulation. The oocyte in a growing follicle is a primary oocyte, and it stays one through all of follicle growth. It does not become a secondary oocyte until ovulation, when the factors that inhibit meiosis are suppressed or removed as a result of the LH surge. The surge triggers resumption of meiosis, and the first meiotic division is complete by the time the oocyte is ovulated. The second meiotic division is completed in the fallopian tube. In class he named the block: the antrum's fluid holds plasma proteins, growth factors and factors that arrest the cell cycle, among them oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), which keeps the oocyte "in a locked state" until ovulation. The LH surge lowers OMI, so meiosis resumes. The L14 histology lecture adds the detail behind that: the ovulated secondary oocyte waits at metaphase of meiosis two and finishes the division only if a sperm fertilizes it, which happens in the tube. Preovulatory Graafian follicles have a high expression of LH receptors, and the surge does two things to them: it triggers resumption of meiosis and follicular rupture. The egg is released from the dominant follicle typically 24 to 36 hours after the surge. In response to the surge, collagenases rise and weaken the follicular wall, and prostaglandins rise and increase blood flow, so the mature follicle becomes weak enough to rupture. In class he summed up the surge's effects on the follicle as three: proteases such as collagenase degrade the collagen in its wall, prostaglandins raise its blood flow, and oocyte maturation inhibitor falls, so the first meiotic division can finish. 6 Estrogen and progesterone on the lining and the cervical mucus (and the myometrium, on the slide) Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Watery cervical mucus decreases, and the mucus becomes thick. The speaker notes say GnRH goes sky high, and rising GnRH can lead to hot flashes. In class he said hot flashes have been linked to that GnRH peak, though research linking the symptoms to the hormone levels is still going on. 9 The follicle's life: granulosa cells (primary), then layers and theca cells (secondary), an antrum, one dominant follicle; the corpus luteum, its 14 days and menses Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Watch the names. These slides call the many-layered follicle with a theca the secondary follicle, and the follicle with an antrum the Graafian follicle. The L14 histology lecture names the same stages differently: early primary for one cuboidal layer, late primary for several layers with a theca, secondary for the follicle with an antrum, and mature Graafian for the large follicle about to ovulate. The order of events is the same in both, so learn the sequence and not just the labels. In class Dr. Madison called the in-between follicle with an antrum tertiary or antral and kept Graafian for the dominant follicle about to ovulate, close to L14's names. Primordial The resting follicle; none moves on before puberty Can wait 13 to 50 years Primary A single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells around the oocyte Granulosa cells start expressing FSH receptors Secondary (the histology lecture's late primary) Multiple granulosa layers and a theca (interna and externa) Theca interna develops LH receptors; growth driven by oocyte growth factors Graafian, with an antrum (the histology lecture's secondary, then mature Graafian) A fluid-filled antrum; a few start each cycle, one becomes dominant High LH receptor expression before ovulation Corpus luteum The ruptured follicle's remains, mostly granulosa cells Secretes steroid hormones, mainly progesterone in the luteal phase 10 The default pathway: no AMH (Müllerian ducts form), no testosterone (Wolffian ducts regress), no DHT (female external genitalia) Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this No AMH: the Müllerian ducts form the fallopian tubes and uterus. No testosterone: the Wolffian ducts regress. No DHT: the external genitalia form as female. In class he added the third missing male hormone: with no DHT (and no testosterone), the external genitalia form as female, also by default, and the Müllerian ducts go on to form the fallopian tubes and the uterus. "What you need to understand," he said, is that without testosterone, DHT and anti-Müllerian hormone, "the default pathway is female reproductive development." 11 Amenorrhea: primary (genetic, Turner syndrome) versus secondary (pregnancy, lactation, menopause, hyperprolactinemia; prolactin turns GnRH down) Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Primary amenorrhea is usually genetic (his example: Turner syndrome, an X partly or completely lost, malformed ovaries). Secondary amenorrhea: menopause, pregnancy, lactation and hyperprolactinemia (a pituitary tumor), the last two because prolactin turns GnRH down. In class he described primary amenorrhea as usually genetic, with Turner syndrome as his example: one X chromosome is partly or completely lost, the ovaries are fully or partly malformed, the follicles can't go through their staged, cyclic development, and the person can't reproduce. So Turner syndrome sits under disorders of sexual differentiation on the slide and under primary amenorrhea in class; both are right. He then explained each cause of secondary amenorrhea: in menopause estradiol is lost; in pregnancy LH and FSH lose their normal cycle; in lactation, and with a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumor, prolactin is high, and prolactin turns GnRH down, so FSH, LH and the sex steroids fall and the cycle stops. Also flagged in class Make the two-column table: follicular (days 0 to 14, proliferative, the growing follicle, estrogen, the lining grows, watery stretchy mucus that helps sperm, estradiol's negative feedback, working toward fertilization) against luteal (days 14 to 28, secretory, the corpus luteum, progesterone, proliferation slows, more vessels and glycogen, thick mucus, a slight rise in temperature, working toward implantation). Progesterone: negative only. Estradiol: negative through the follicular phase, positive at midcycle once it passes about 200 pg/mL. Three estrogens, three stages of life: estradiol (reproductive years, the ovary), estriol (pregnancy), estrone (menopause). After menopause the estrogen is estrone, made from adrenal DHEA, and it is not nearly as potent as estradiol. Primary follicle: the follicular cells around the oocyte become cuboidal granulosa cells. Secondary follicle: the granulosa cells proliferate into many layers and theca cells appear on the outside. You can skip Skip the rest of the steroid pathway's enzymes; know the two he named and which hormone and cell each belongs to. Don't memorize the names of the in-between follicles (tertiary or antral); know the order, that several grow each cycle, that one Graafian follicle becomes dominant and releases the egg, and that the rest regress. Skip slide 33 (estrogen and progesterone on the skin, memory, mammary glands, GI motility, the brain and the heart). The menopause slide's symptoms right after it still count.
